newsitem.title: GERMANY: German investors could avoid a non-EMU Britain.
newsitem.headline: German investors could avoid a non-EMU Britain.

text.p: German companies may steer clear of investing in Britain after the 1999 start of European currency union if London decides not to take part and they could instead favour EMU members, analysts said on Friday.

The analysts' reaction came in the wake of comments made on Wednesday by the head of the Japanese car firm Toyota that it would restrict its investments in Britain if it does not join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.

"With the introduction of the single European currency the affected area, the so-called Euroland, will become more interesting for investors, who will tend to look there rather than outside the area when making decisions," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
Analysts agree that the removal of exchange rate fluctuations within Euroland would leave Britain isolated.
Even if sterling performs strongly against the euro after EMU, investors long-term are more interested in currency stability than what could be only short-term gains.

"The U.K. will be pushed into developing an outside role. The City of London has already voiced fears that euro-related transactions will pass it by. Transport costs and language barriers are no longer really an issue, but exchange rate risk is a problem," said Grebe.
Robert Willis, German analyst at Schroder Securities in London, said: "You would need an extremely attractive investment environment in the U.K. to offset the currency risk post-EMU."
German companies remain cautious on making pronouncements on the issue, adopting a wait-and-see stance, and have not made any changes in investment policy for the time being.

The German Association of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) said that it sees no reason for making its investments in Britain dependent on EMU membership, and said that a favourable exchange rate could even benefit German companies.
However, with two years to go before the proposed start of EMU and with a British election on the cards soon, companies were loathe to make any firm post-EMU forecasts.

Axel Nitschke, economist at DIHT, said that Britain was the most important country for German foreign investment in 1995. Of a total of 48 billion marks ($29 billion) invested abroad, 10.6 billion was spent in Britain.
Nitschke said that the main reason for this was the low labour costs in Britain, which were half the levels of Germany and start-up time was twice as quick in Britain.
However, the forthcoming election in Britain could see the Labour Party coming to power.
With a Labour government in power, analysts see Britain possibly signing the EU's Social Charter, which aims to formally enshrine labour rights in Europe and which the U.K. has declined to join.

Labour has also said it will introduce a minimum wage, which is seen as inevitably driving wage costs higher. Some analysts also fear an increase in National Insurance payments, which would function as a de facto tax hike.
All of which contributes to making the U.K. a more expensive site to locate.
"Ford has cut back its workforce in the U.K. because it is a lot easier than doing it anywhere else -- it's more difficult in Spain and in Germany it's impossible," said Willis.
"A change in U.K. labour laws would add a question mark on companies setting up -- marginal investment becomes even more marginal," said Willis.
Tax reforms at home in Germany will also encourage German investors to stay put.

"Germany has seen a lot of movement abroad and domestic tax reforms may encourage more companies to stay at home. This may lead to German firms viewing the U.K. as part of a broader picture, along the lines of Eastern Europe," said Willis.
Grebe believes that German tax reform was a direct result of the move towards currency union and says that if exchange rate risk disappears, then taxation and labour costs come strongly into play.
"In my scenario, the British will join EMU after two or three years as the disadvantages become too obvious -- the U.K. is too pragmatic not to," said Grebe.
